title_eng: Pre-processing of Photoplethysmographic Waveform for Amplitude Regularization
abstract:
This study is aimed to develop a post-processing method to regularize amplitude of PPG waveforms and evaluate the per -
formance of the algorithm. The proposed procedure for regularizing amplitude consists of extracting the signal envelopes 
based on time-domain filtering, generating a compensation curve, and reconstructing the waveform. The proposed technique 
was evaluated with respect to dispersion and waveform fluctuation by means of coefficients of variation (CV) and a scaling 
exponent of detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA). Other criteria included the detection performances of major features such 
as upper and lower fiducial points and maximum dV/dt. In developing this method, we used a clinical dataset that comprised 
74,225 beats. By applying reconstruction algorithm, the %CV and the scaling exponent of DFA were significantly decreased 
from 115.4 to 71.4 and from 1.029 to 0.836, respectively in peak amplitude. In valley amplitude, they were also decreased 
from 38.3 to 13.2 and from 0.993 to 0.713, respectively. Moreover, sensitivity of maximum dV/ dt point, upper and lower 
peak detection are increased by 8.50, 2.72 and 5.21% after reconstruction, respectively. Our results clearly showed that the 
proposed reconstruction technique could reduce amplitude fluctuation and improve detection of fiducial points.

Abstract
This study is aimed to develop a post-processing method to regularize amplitude of PPG waveforms and evaluate the per -
formance of the algorithm. The proposed procedure for regularizing amplitude consists of extracting the signal envelopes 
based on time-domain filtering, generating a compensation curve, and reconstructing the waveform. The proposed technique 
was evaluated with respect to dispersion and waveform fluctuation by means of coefficients of variation (CV) and a scaling 
exponent of detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA). Other criteria included the detection performances of major features such 
as upper and lower fiducial points and maximum dV/dt. In developing this method, we used a clinical dataset that comprised 
74,225 beats. By applying reconstruction algorithm, the %CV and the scaling exponent of DFA were significantly decreased 
from 115.4 to 71.4 and from 1.029 to 0.836, respectively in peak amplitude. In valley amplitude, they were also decreased 
from 38.3 to 13.2 and from 0.993 to 0.713, respectively. Moreover, sensitivity of maximum dV/ dt point, upper and lower 
peak detection are increased by 8.50, 2.72 and 5.21% after reconstruction, respectively. Our results clearly showed that the 
proposed reconstruction technique could reduce amplitude fluctuation and improve detection of fiducial points.
Keywords Feature detection · Low perfusion · Motion artifact · Photoplethysmography · Physiological signal processing
1 Introduction
The optical physiological monitoring technique photop-
lethysmography (PPG) is a practical and effective tool in 
the personal health monitoring because the PPG device 
has a simple structure and provides an easy, noninvasive 
way to measure physiological signals such as pulse rate 
or even autonomic functions. In recent years, PPG has 
been adopted as way to track one’s health or fitness in the 
form of wearable devices such as the Jawbone, the Fitbit 
wristband, Samsung’s Galaxy Watch, or the Apple Watch. 
Such devices have an optical transmitter and a receiver to 
measure the PPG signal. Although PPG can provide sev -
eral advantages, such as ease of implementation or lack 
of electrical interference. In general, the PPG waveform 
consists of a pulsatile component (AC) and a non-pulsatile 
component (DC). The AC component, which is typically 
around 1 Hz, depending on heart rate, reflects changes in 
blood volume according to the mechanical activity of the 
heart (e.g., systole and diastole). Because the AC com-
ponent is influenced by circulatory factors, conditions of 
the heart and blood vessels can cause changes in the PPG 
waveform. For example, cardiac or vascular problems, 
such as poor circulation due to vascular insufficiency, 
could degrade the AC component. The DC component of 
the PPG waveform indicates basal light absorption, which 
is reflected in very gradual changes in the waveform. Light 
is scattered and absorbed by anatomical structures such 
as bone and tissue at the site of measurement and non-
pulsatile blood, which includes not only the non-pulsatile 
component of arterial blood but also the venous blood. 
Because the DC component of PPG depends on the whole 
process of traveling light, numerous constituents could 
induce unexpected changes, including such factors as skin 
pigmentation, length of the optical path, ambient light,

sensor type, sensor position, autonomic nervous system 
activity, vasomotor activity and vasoconstrictor waves, 
Traube-Hering-Mayer (THM) waves, thermoregulation, 
respiratory activity, and anatomical structures [1 –3]. In 
other words, the amplitude of the PPG waveform, which 
represents the sum of the AC and DC components, is usu-
ally subject to numerous effects, thus generating amplitude 
fluctuations that are regarded as noise or distortion. Espe-
cially, in mobile healthcare environment, PPG waveform 
is severely distorted by motion artifact as well as ambient 
noise. These artifacts cause a baseline fluctuation or an 
amplitude variation of signal, making it difficult to detect 
important clinical information. For example, motion arti-
fact that can make an abrupt change of DC levels is an 
inevitable factor in ambulatory condition, however, motion 
artifact-induced amplitude change is usually much larger 
than signal amplitude, and finally it causes saturation and 
loss of PPG signals. These situations had been frequently 
found in the clinical setting, but now, with the expansion 
of PPG-based technologies, they occur in everyday, practi -
cal settings as well.
Many techniques have been developed to assess the sig-
nal quality of PPG and to improve the analyzed result’s 
accuracy [4 –7]. To assess waveform distortion, Couceiro 
proposed motion artifact detection algorithm based on the 
analysis of the variations in the time and period domain 
characteristics of the PPG signal, and showed the 83% 
of sensitivity and 93% of specificity [4 ]. Sukor proposed 
morphology-based pulse quality assessment technique and 
showed 89 ± 10% of sensitivity, 77 ± 19% of specificity 
and 83 ± 11% of accuracy, respectively [8 ]. Dao proposed 
TifMA based on time–frequency analysis [9 ] and showed 
higher amplitude fluctuation detection accuracy compared 
with Hjorth parameters [10], kurtosis-Shannon Entropy 
[11] and time-domain variability-SVM approach [12]. 
Recently, noise interference-based method [ 13], proba -
bilistic neural network-based personalized motion artifact 
detection method [14], and morphology- and correlation-
based methods [15] were also introduced for PPG signal 
quality assessment. As a reconstruction or a noise reduc-
tion method, methods had been developed based on adap-
tive filtering with multiple wavelength PPG to enhance 
the PPG waveform in cases of having low perfusion and 
motion artifact [16, 17]. Though these methods have 
improved performance compared with previous methods, 
the adaptive-filtering method is based on multiple light 
sources and is therefore not suitable for PPG, which is 
based on a single light source. As another approach, Kim 
showed the possibility of independent component analysis 
(ICA) in motion artifact reduction [6 ]. In Salehizadeh’s 
research, iterative motion artifact removal (IMARS) has 
better performance in heart rate and SpO2 detection in 
noisy environments [18]. Li also proposed double median 
filter-based slight motion artifact reduction method in 
transmitted and reflected PPG [19].
Also, to remove artifacts with hardware, Warren has 
attempted to change the measurement channel in the hard-
ware to remove motion noises, and some performance 
improvements have been reported [20]. Kasbekar proposed 
key design features to reduce motion artifacts for a mobile 
reflectance PPG and found that sensor placement, contact 
force and sensor- to -skin adhesion or relative motion when 
combined with force are the most important in reducing 
motion artifacts [21]. Previous studies comparing periodic 
motion artifact removal performance based on sensor-skin 
contact measurement with interferometry and movement 
measured with an accelerometer have shown that motion 
artifact is more effectively remove when an acceleration 
sensor is used with frequency locked loop (FLL) [22]. 
Removing the amplitude fluctuation after reconstruction of 
the signal can increase the accuracy of fiducial point detec-
tion, which is an important factor for utilization. The pur -
pose of our study is to develop technique for reducing the 
amplitude fluctuation of PPG waveforms without the need 
for additional hardware features. Amplitude stabilization 
could improve feature detection performance by regulating 
the signal levels as well as clinical diagnostic accuracy by 
providing accurate waveform information.
2 Materials and Methods
2.1 Designing the Gain Compensation Curve
The algorithm we propose basically consists of extracting 
the waveform envelope, generating the gain compensation 
curve and reconstructing the waveform. Figure  1 shows 
the overall procedure of waveform regularization. In the 
first stage, we remove the signal offset and linear trend. To 
remove the signal trend, we calculated the least-squares 
fit of the data to a straight line and subtracted the result-
ing function of the data. After removing the trend, a finite 
impulse response (FIR) band-pass filter (BPF) was used to 
extract the dominant frequency component of a PPG wave-
form. The frequency spectrum, including the dominant fre-
quency of the PPG, reflects the heart rate and its harmonic 
components. This dominant frequency component could be 
represented as a sinusoidal wave within a time domain and 
constitutes most of the PPG signal’s energy. In other words, 
it indicates the overall low-frequency amplitude variations 
of the PPG waveform in a sinusoidal pattern. On the other 
hand, harmonics are related to abrupt changes in the wave-
form and therefore contribute to the reconstruction of high-
frequency variations in the waveform. Previous research
